lesson.title: Counting People Who Could Not Be Citizens
lesson.summary: The Three-Fifths Compromise settled a bitter dispute at the Constitutional Convention by counting each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for both representation and taxation, embedding slavery's political power directly into the new Constitution.
lesson.body:
Once the Great Compromise had settled how representation in the House would be divided, apportioned according to each state's population, delegates ran straight into a second, thornier question that the first compromise had only postponed. Slavery had existed throughout the colonies since the seventeenth century, but by 1787 it was concentrated heavily in the southern states, where enslaved people made up a large share of the total population in places like South Carolina and Virginia.

Southern delegates wanted enslaved people counted as part of a state's population when determining how many seats that state would get in the House of Representatives, since more population meant more political power. Yet many of those same delegates did not want enslaved people counted at all when it came to calculating how much in direct taxes a state owed to the national government, since more population there meant a larger tax bill. Northern delegates, representing states where slavery was less economically central and increasingly unpopular, argued the opposite on both counts, since counting enslaved people for representation without counting them as citizens with rights struck many as indefensible.

The compromise that emerged split this contradiction down the middle rather than resolving it on principle. Each enslaved person would count as three-fifths of a free person for the purposes of both representation in the House and direct taxation, a formula that had actually been proposed earlier, in 1783, as part of an unsuccessful attempt to amend the Articles of Confederation's taxation rules. Delegates simply adapted that existing numerical formula for the new Constitution, and it became part of Article I, Section 2.

The compromise was never framed by its authors as a statement about anyone's humanity, and it satisfied almost no one on moral grounds. It was a political bargain designed to hold the convention together and secure southern states' support for the new Constitution, since without some accommodation on slavery, delegates from South Carolina and Georgia in particular threatened to walk away from the entire project. Related provisions negotiated around the same time protected the Atlantic slave trade from federal interference until at least 1808 and required states to return people who had escaped slavery to their enslavers.

The practical effect was to substantially boost southern political power, since it inflated southern states' seats in the House and, later, their votes in the Electoral College, without granting the enslaved people being counted any rights, freedom, or voice at all. That imbalance would shape American politics for decades, giving slaveholding states outsized influence in national debates right up through the growing sectional crisis of the nineteenth century.
